name: EgoScale
summary: EgoScale trains a flow-based VLA on over 20,854 hours of action-labelled egocentric human video - more than 20x the largest prior effort - and reports a log-linear scaling law between human data volume and validation loss, arguing that human-to-robot dexterous transfer is fundamentally a scaling phenomenon rather than an architecture problem. The pipeline has three stages: large-scale human pretraining, aligned human-robot mid-training, and task-specific post-training from roughly 100 teleoperated demonstrations. Hand motion is recovered by 3D hand-pose extraction, with MANUS gloves supplying precise motion ground truth for the alignment stage, and a unified human-robot action space is handled by embodiment-specific adapters on a shared trunk. On a 22-DoF robotic hand the method improves average success rate by 54% over baseline, supports one-shot adaptation to new tasks with minimal robot supervision, and transfers to lower-DoF hands, which is the evidence offered that the learned motor prior is embodiment-agnostic. Submitted 18 February 2026 by authors at NVIDIA GEAR, UC Berkeley, UT Austin, Stanford, Georgia Tech and UMD.
innovation: Action labels on human video at a scale where a clean log-linear loss curve appears, turning 'collect more human video' into a forecastable engineering decision rather than a hope.
A three-stage human-pretrain / human-robot-align / task-post-train recipe that separates the motor prior from the embodiment, so the expensive stage is paid once.
Embodiment-specific adapters over a shared flow-based trunk, which is what lets one prior serve hands with different degrees of freedom.
matters: It is the first result to put a scaling law on the human-video axis specifically, and the industrial human-data programmes that followed within six months - Dyna-2 at a million hours, Figure's Index - are arguing the same thesis at larger scale.
Dexterous multi-fingered manipulation is where teleoperated robot data is most expensive, so it is the setting where substituting human video pays most.
limits: The headline scaling law is on validation loss; the on-robot evidence is a 54% relative improvement on one 22-DoF hand, not a curve over many platforms.
Stage-2 alignment depends on MANUS glove capture, so reproducing the pipeline is not simply a matter of scraping more video.
Code was listed as coming soon on the project page and no official NVIDIA release has been confirmed, so the result is not independently reproduced.
lineage: Takes PH2D and EgoDex's use of action-labelled egocentric human video as robot supervision and asks the scaling question of it, with LAPA's action-free pretraining as the alternative it implicitly argues against.
